item.title: Exclusive video shows Philippine medical evacuation near Ren'ai Jiao conducted under China Coast Guard supervision
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-10 17:49:00
Exclusive video shows Philippine medical evacuation near Ren’ai Jiao conducted under China Coast Guard supervision By Feng Fan Published: Oct 10, 2026 05:49 PM A Philippine rigid inflatable boat from BRP Sierra Madre transfers an injured personnel to another rigid inflatable boat under China Coast Guard vessels’ supervision on October 8, 2026. Exclusive footage obtained by the Global Times shows that a Philippine medical evacuation near China’s Ren’ai Jiao on Thursday was carried out with China’s permission and remained under China Coast Guard (CCG) supervision throughout the operation. The footage shows CCG vessel 5306 promptly warned the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) vessel 4409 to leave after the Philippine vessel entered waters near Ren’ai Jiao without China’s permission. On humanitarian grounds, a rigid inflatable boat launched from PCG vessel 4409 was subsequently allowed to proceed to an area designated by the Chinese side, guided and monitored by a Chinese rigid inflatable boat. At the designated area, the Philippine rigid inflatable boat transferred an injured person from the BRP Sierra Madre, the Philippine ship illegally grounded at Ren’ai Jiao, with Chinese rigid inflatable boats and coast guard vessel supervising the operation, the footage shows. A PCG spokesperson claimed that CCG vessels had “obstructed” the evacuation mission, made dangerous maneuvers near a PCG vessel and used water cannons. China allows humanitarian medical evacuations, personnel rotations and resupply missions involving the Philippine ship illegally grounded at Ren’ai Jiao in China’s Nansha Qundao, Chen Xiangmiao, a researcher at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies, told the Global Times. However, the Philippines has repeatedly used resupply missions to deliver construction materials to reinforce the ship’s hull, seeking to use the vessel to illegally occupy the reef, Chen said. China therefore imposes controls on deliveries, and such resupply activities require its permission, he said. These resupply and personnel transfer operations have long been conducted under Chinese supervision and control, Chen said. Yet the Philippines sent a coast guard vessel for the medical evacuation without prior communication with China on Thursday, then portrayed itself as the victim to seek sympathy and challenge China’s territorial integrity, he said. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning on Friday rejected Philippine claims that China had disrupted the medical evacuation, stressing that China would not waver in responding to any provocation and safeguarding territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests. At a regular press briefing, Mao said that a PCG vessel had intruded into waters adjacent to Ren’ai Jiao in Nansha Qundao of China without China’s permission on Thursday morning. Mao said that following communication between the two sides, on humanitarian grounds, China gave timely permission to the Philippine side to evacuate the injured person by small boat and provided necessary assistance. Instead of acknowledging China’s facilitation, individual Philippine officials have distorted facts and wrongfully accused China without showing the whole picture to the public, Mao said. This once again reveals their intention of provoking China and staging publicity stunts, which is rather despicable, she said. Mao’s remarks followed a statement issued by the CCG on Thursday evening. CCG spokesperson Jiang Lue said that PCG vessel 4409 had traveled to waters near Ren’ai Jiao that day to evacuate an injured person from the Philippine warship illegally grounded there. Jiang added that, on humanitarian grounds, China had immediately allowed the injured person to be transferred by small boat. The CCG handled the matter in accordance with laws and regulations and provided necessary assistance, he said. Jiang said the Philippine side’s remarks disregarded the facts, distorted the truth and sought to mislead the public. China has indisputable sovereignty over Nansha Qundao, including Ren’ai Jiao, and their adjacent waters, he said, warning the Philippine side to immediately stop its infringements, provocations and dissemination of false claims.

item.title: China launches platform for foreign-related legal services, to accelerate research on dedicated legislation to protect Chinese enterprises' overseas interests
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-10 17:29:00
China's Ministry of Justice holds a press conference on strengthening foreign-related legal services and the official launch of the “Lex Com” platform on October 10, 2026. Photo: Ministry of Justice China's Ministry of Justice announced on Saturday the official launch of "Lex Com," a nationwide platform designed to provide legal services to Chinese companies and citizens operating overseas. Foreign-related legal services are an important component of and provide strong support for advancing the rule of law in foreign-related affairs, and play an indispensable role in safeguarding China's overseas interests and the rights and interests of Chinese enterprises and citizens going global, Vice Minister of Justice Wu Yanjun said at a press conference on the same day. The platform offers practical tools, including legal and regulatory searches and consultations on specialized legal issues, to address the needs of Chinese businesses and citizens and enhance their capacity to handle foreign-related legal matters, according to the ministry. The platform provides integrated access to a comprehensive range of legal resources, covering foreign-related laws and regulations, regional and country-specific legal guides, foreign law searches and compilations of representative cases. It includes 207 Chinese laws, 231 administrative regulations and 1,372 departmental rules concerning foreign-related affairs. It also provides over 1,500 legal resources covering 187 countries and regions worldwide, including Chinese translations of 976 foreign laws, 512 country-specific legal guides and 140 typical cases. The platform also offers tailored legal consultations on practical legal questions through two channels: an AI-powered agent that draws on the platform's resources to provide prompt answers for reference, and a consultation service where a professional team reviews users' questions and provides considered responses. Meanwhile, it strengthens corporate legal teams through coordinated resources. By integrating legal resources across jurisdictions and fields, Lex Com supports corporate legal teams and helps Chinese companies operating overseas develop legal talent. It also integrates online and offline services, with training videos for heads of legal affairs at foreign-related enterprises available for on-demand viewing. China has amended the Foreign Trade Law and the Maritime Law, and is currently revising the Customs Law, as part of efforts to improve the environment for openness and cooperation, and advance high-standard opening up. As Chinese companies and citizens expand their overseas activities, conducting business and other activities abroad has become increasingly common. A key priority in strengthening the rule of law in foreign-related affairs is to safeguard China's overseas assets and protect the overseas interests of its companies and citizens. Wu said the ministry will address new economic and social development needs during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30), coordinate efforts to advance foreign-related legislative projects concerning international judicial assistance in civil and commercial matters, overseas labor cooperation and overseas contracted projects, and accelerate research on dedicated legislation to protect overseas interests and safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of businesses and citizens. Global Times

item.title: China, EU demonstrate willingness and wisdom to resolve trade differences through dialogue; EU to consider possible facilitation measures for China: MOFCOM official
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-10 17:03:00
Photo: screenshot of the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) The outcomes and consensus reached by China and the EU fully demonstrate that the two sides have the willingness and wisdom to manage and properly resolve differences through dialogue and consultation, effectively preventing the escalation of frictions, an official with China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) said on Saturday, noting that the two sides have agreed to convene the third meeting of China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism in March 2027. Chinese Minister of Commerce Wang Wentao and European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic jointly chaired the second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism from Thursday to Friday in Beijing, according to the MOFCOM. The two sides held equal, professional and constructive talks on trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property rights and WTO reform, reviewed consultations and progress made since the mechanism's first meeting, and reached consensus on a number of outcomes, the MOFCOM official said in a statement on the ministry's website. The two sides held intensive consultations based on the principles of mutual respect, equality and mutual benefit. They discussed how to address each other's concerns on an equal footing, expand two-way market access and promote a dynamic balance in China-EU trade, covering sectors including medical devices, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, inverters, and agricultural and food products, the official said. The two sides agreed to make use of the trade monitoring mechanism, explore the possibility of reducing tariffs on certain goods under WTO rules, and hold technical discussions on the EU's Foreign Subsidies Regulation, with a view to creating a fair, transparent and predictable environment for China-EU trade and investment cooperation. Building on previous sound cooperation, the two sides expressed willingness to exchange views on market access in sectors such as medical devices and agricultural products, and to maintain communication on the EU's guidance document on financing for inverter projects, as well as regulations concerning cosmetics and pharmaceuticals. On trade in EVs and hybrid vehicles, the two sides held in-depth discussions based on the principles of respecting facts, non-discrimination and compliance with WTO rules. The discussions helped avoid an escalation of tensions, safeguard the actual export interests of Chinese enterprises and maintain the stable development of China-EU hybrid vehicle trade, according to the official. The two sides also reviewed the previously agreed general guidance document on price undertakings in the EU's anti-subsidy case against Chinese EVs. The EU side will actively advance the relevant procedures for companies' price undertakings and reviews in the EV case. On export controls, the two sides agreed to further leverage their export control dialogue mechanism, strengthen policy communication and maintain stable and smooth global industrial and supply chains. Both sides reiterated their commitment to addressing each other's concerns in the field of export controls. The EU side will continue to work toward progress in resolving key individual licensing cases involving China in the dual-use sector. The two sides explored the possibility of introducing facilitation measures for compliant trade in dual-use items, while the EU side will consider possible facilitation measures for China. The two sides also agreed to strengthen communication on delisting issues related to sanctions lists in the field of export controls, and to support and substantively initiate reciprocal delisting procedures within their respective legal frameworks. Looking ahead, both sides saw considerable potential for cooperation in new energy, artificial intelligence, trade in services, the digital economy, and green and low-carbon development, and agreed to explore new opportunities and expand areas of cooperation. The two sides also agreed to explore two-way investment cooperation. China reiterated its welcome for EU companies to invest and do business in China and its commitment to improving the business environment. China also expressed its expectation that the EU will provide a fair, transparent and predictable business environment for Chinese companies, effectively protect their legitimate rights and interests, and strengthen their confidence and expectations regarding investment and operations in Europe. On intellectual property rights, the two sides expressed willingness to deepen exchanges and expand cooperation. China also expressed its hope that the EU would attach importance to China's concerns and actively work toward resolving them. They agreed on the need to set phased objectives and continue to make full use of the China-EU intellectual property working group as the main channel for deepening cooperation and monitoring progress. On WTO reform, the two sides stressed the value of a rules-based multilateral trading system, expressed support for WTO reform and emphasized the importance of complying with WTO rules. They agreed to further strengthen communication and cooperation in an open and constructive manner and discuss all relevant issues concerning WTO reform, with a view to making substantive progress. The two sides reaffirmed their positions as key trading partners and agreed to address economic and trade differences and each other's concerns in a balanced manner within the framework of WTO rules, explore deeper mutually beneficial cooperation, and promote China-EU trade balance in an upward and forward direction. Both sides agreed that the consultation mechanism has operated smoothly and efficiently, and that the second meeting marked a new starting point rather than an endpoint, the MOFCOM official said. Both sides also agreed that stable and healthy China-EU economic and trade relations benefit businesses and people on both sides, serve their common interests, and inject certainty and positive momentum into global economic growth and the stability of industrial and supply chains. The two sides agreed to step up efforts to implement the outcomes reached at the second meeting and maintain close communication at various levels. They also agreed to hold a ministerial-level video meeting in January 2027, ahead of the third meeting of the consultation mechanism scheduled for March 2027. Jian Junbo, director of the Center for China-Europe Relations at Fudan University, told the Global Times on Saturday that the outcomes of the latest China-EU trade talks were encouraging, with the two sides reaching consensus on issues including electric vehicles, intellectual property protection and WTO reform. "The progress on EVs, particularly hybrid vehicles, is especially noteworthy, given the EU's concerns over the issue," Jian told the Global Times. "The progress reflects the economic realities and deep interdependence between China and the EU. Against the backdrop of rising US protectionism, both sides rely heavily on international trade and openness. Neither side would benefit from a more serious economic confrontation, which would only hurt their own economies," Jian said. On trade facilitation, Jian said the progress could help boost bilateral trade.

item.title: The louder protectionism roars, the more precious China-EU dialogue becomes: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-10 00:52:00
China EU Photo:VCG At a time when global challenges continue to emerge, the significance of China-EU relations has long extended beyond the bilateral sphere. By continuously deepening their economic ties and shared interests, China and the EU can not only unleash the innovative potential of their respective markets but also reinforce each other's development and contribute to global economic recovery. From Thursday to Friday, China and the EU held the second meeting of their bilateral trade and investment consultation mechanism in Beijing. The two sides engaged in pragmatic and productive discussions, reaching a 16-point consensus covering trade and investment balances, export controls, intellectual property rights and reform of the World Trade Organization (WTO). Against the backdrop of a sluggish global economic recovery and undercurrents of anti-globalization, this is a pragmatic step to properly handle bilateral differences and a crucial display of responsibility by China and the EU in injecting stability and certainty into the global economy amid turbulent times. A closer look at this list reveals its core value: anchored in rules-based governance and bridged by mutual trust, it demonstrates the political wisdom to manage differences and steer China-EU economic and trade relations toward greater stability and balance. The first item on the list states that both sides will continue to explore the possibility of reducing tariffs on certain products within the WTO framework. In the hybrid vehicle trade sector, which has attracted significant public attention, the two sides agreed to reach a mutual understanding in a manner consistent with WTO rules, providing a pathway to ease the previously deadlocked trade dispute. In the field of export controls, China expressed its willingness to continue facilitating export license approvals for rare earths and permanent magnets bound for the EU through a "green channel" mechanism. The two sides also included "advance notifications before items are added to control lists" in the consensus list. This arrangement improves the transparency in listing and delisting procedures, helping to reduce misjudgments and stabilize expectations. This list covers a significant portion of the current challenges and bottlenecks in economic and trade relations between China and the EU, and the consensus reached by both sides demonstrates that no matter how complex trade frictions may be, pragmatic solutions can always be found as long as both sides uphold the spirit of dialogue and adhere to equal-footed consultation. The convergence of interests is the inevitable outcome of economic globalization and more so a powerful engine driving common prosperity for China, the EU, and the world at large. In 2025, China-EU trade in goods exceeded $800 billion, with their combined economic output accounting for over one-third of the global total, bilateral trade volume making up nearly one-quarter of the world's total, and nearly half of bilateral trade consisting of intermediate goods. The long-standing pattern of "trade surpluses in China and profits in Europe" has made the two sides a community of shared interests, with each deeply intertwined with the other. This also demonstrates that as long as China and the EU work together, the synergies they generate will far outweigh the narrow calculations of a zero-sum game, creating vast new opportunities for industrial upgrading and improving the well-being of their peoples. Protectionism cannot enhance competitiveness, while decoupling and severing supply chains will only harm others without benefiting oneself. By continuously deepening their economic ties and shared interests, China and the EU can not only unleash the innovative potential of their respective markets but also reinforce each other's development and contribute to global economic recovery. As a major strategic force in the world, Europe should uphold its tradition of multilateralism and strategic autonomy, rather than allow itself to be swept up in the tide of protectionism and the excessive securitization of economic issues. At the moment, unilateralism is on the rise, with certain major powers frequently imposing sanctions in an attempt to weaponize economic and trade issues. Europe has a deep-rooted tradition of free trade and should not simply follow the crowd, much less turn security anxieties into trade barriers. As China has repeatedly and sincerely pointed out, the EU should remain committed to openness, cooperation and free trade, abide by WTO rules, not resort to protectionist tools at every turn, and, above all, refrain from politicizing and excessively securitizing economic and trade issues - so as to avoid pursuing misguided policies that will ultimately backfire on itself. China is not the root cause of the EU's problems, but a partner in addressing them. Faced with a complex external environment, Europe can only truly safeguard its fundamental interests amid changes unseen in a century by taking a long-term view of the economic and trade relations between China and the EU and adhering to equal-footed dialogue and consultation. Looking ahead to future arrangements for institutionalized consultations, China and the EU should overcome obstacles through sustained dialogue and work together to provide stability and certainty to the world. The two sides have agreed to hold the third regular meeting under the mechanism in March 2027 and maintain close communication in the meantime, including a ministerial-level video meeting in January 2027. Such institutionalized and regular arrangements provide an important safeguard for bridging differences and deepening cooperation. At a time when global challenges continue to emerge, the significance of China-EU relations has long extended beyond the bilateral sphere. In the face of an international landscape marked by intertwined turbulence and transformation, China and the EU should be partners that build mutual trust rather than systemic rivals, and promoters of cooperation rather than instigators of friction. We look forward to both China and the EU seizing this opportunity presented by the consultations to continue deepening cooperation based on equal dialogue and mutual benefit, translating more consensus into concrete actions, ensuring that the benefits of China-EU economic and trade cooperation continue to benefit the people of both sides, and injecting more warmth and confidence into a global economy fraught with uncertainty.

item.title: Chinese national killed in attack on construction site in Nigeria's Kebbi State: report
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-10 00:33:00
Map of Kebbi State in Nigeria Photo: screenshot from a Channels Television report A Chinese national was killed along with two local security personnel in an attack on a construction site in Nigeria's Kebbi State on Thursday, the Xinhua News Agency reported on Friday, citing local police. According to Xinhua, the Kebbi State Police Command said in a statement on Friday that armed men entered the area from neighboring Sokoto State and attacked a construction site, killing a foreign national and two local security personnel. Police confirmed to Xinhua on Friday that the foreign national killed in the attack was a Chinese citizen, according to the report. Two other people were injured in the attack and taken to hospital for treatment, according to the police statement. Police also said they repelled another attack elsewhere in Kebbi State on Thursday, and security forces have been deployed to the affected areas to strengthen security, Xinhua reported. Global Times

item.title: Chinese woman's A$50 thrift-store 'blind box' yields currencies from around the world
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 22:08:00
Coins from various countries are sorted after being taken out of the money jar. Photo: Xiaoxiang Morning Herald report A Chinese woman in Australia got more than she bargained for after spending A$50 ($34.70) on a secondhand money jar, only to discover dozens of currencies from around the world inside, turning the unusual thrift-store purchase into a small profit, Xiaoxiang Morning Herald reported. The woman, who goes by Stella online, told Xiaoxiang Morning Herald that she first came across the jar while casually browsing a charity thrift store on October 1, the first day of China's National Day holidays. She filmed it and posted the video online, where it quickly attracted attention. Curious viewers urged her to find out what was inside, so she returned the next day and bought it. The A$50 jar already showed a few visible banknotes and coins, including a 1-yuan Chinese banknote. Stella explained that the shop was a charity store where donated secondhand items are priced and resold, after some social media users wondered whether the seller was simply trying to make money from the mystery container. Once home, Stella spent more than two hours sorting through the haul. Among the finds were 150,000 Vietnamese dong, S$10, $5, 1 yuan and a variety of old coins. By the time she had separated the currencies into dozens of types, she said, it was already dark outside. A rough calculation put the collection's value at about 421.97 yuan ($63), leaving her more than 180 yuan ahead based on exchange rates. But Stella said she has no plans to cash in. Many of the coins are old and no longer in circulation, and she believes the original owner must have put considerable effort into collecting them. She plans to keep the collection as a souvenir. Global Times

item.title: From Northern Myanmar to the world, an anti-fraud dragnet is tightening
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 21:52:00
A sceenshot of The Demise of Telecom Fraud in Northern Myanmar. Source: CCTV Following its broadcast, the three-part documentary The Demise of Telecom Fraud in Northern Myanmar has caught widespread attention both in China and abroad. This reaction reflects a universal aversion to telecom fraud across the international community and a shared expectation for joint decisive action. Telecom fraud is a global scourge. According to a report by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, economic losses incurred by fraud in East and Southeast Asia, Australia, and other regions reached a staggering $88.3 billion to $114.1 billion in 2025 alone - a figure that even exceeds the GDP of several countries. Perpetrators of telecom fraud have long dug in abroad, directing operations remotely. Meanwhile, funds move in seconds, digital trails are obfuscated through layers of disguise, and victims span multiple nations. Authorities shut down one fraud compound today only to see a new one spring up on another hill tomorrow, or arrest a few ringleaders here while a fresh batch of "agents" emerges elsewhere. This proves a stark reality: without cross-border cooperation - encompassing intelligence sharing, joint arrests, judicial collaboration, and repatriation - anti-fraud efforts are reduced to an endless game of "whack-a-mole," where stamping out one fire only sparks another elsewhere. How to join forces to sever the tentacles of telecom fraud has become a question that is imperative for the international community to answer. The solution demonstrated by China in this battle is to advance international cooperation through concrete action. As revealed in the third episode of the documentary Weaving the Sky Net, Chinese and Myanmar police, leveraging long-standing law enforcement and security cooperation mechanisms, carried out their first joint enforcement operation in Muse town in Myanmar, apprehending 807 telecom fraud suspects in a single sweep and eradicating the final, most stubborn "nail" that had long resisted the special crackdown. Meanwhile, the ministerial-level coordination mechanism established by China, Myanmar, and Thailand in early 2025 launched joint purges against gambling and fraud syndicates in Myanmar's Myawaddy town, carrying out 10 consecutive joint repatriation operations that led to the total demolition of more than 630 buildings in the infamous KK Park. For China, tightening this anti-fraud dragnet is both an essential requirement for safeguarding the property security of its own people and a concrete practice of fulfilling its responsibilities as a major country to build a community with a shared future for humanity. At the law enforcement level, China has repeatedly launched joint crackdown operations with Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, and other countries. At the institutional level, China and its neighboring countries have successively established trilateral coordination mechanisms among China, Myanmar, and Thailand, as well as the Lancang-Mekong law enforcement and security cooperation mechanism. Furthermore, China has helped neighboring nations build law enforcement capacity through material assistance and technical support. Not long ago, the International Alliance Combating Telecom and Cyber Fraud was established in Lianyungang, East China's Jiangsu Province, where representatives from 46 founding countries, 34 observer countries, the United Nations, Interpol, and other bodies issued a joint declaration. This marks a pivotal shift in global anti-fraud efforts - coordinated and advanced by China - from a fragmented "sweeping snow from one's own doorstep" approach to "jointly weaving an integrated global network." Combating telecom fraud is no overnight task, and in the fight against fraud, there are no bystanders. Facing telecom fraud that constantly shifts and mutates, only through broader consensus, more pragmatic measures, and a tighter network can the chain of evil be broken and the peace and well-being of millions of households safeguarded.

item.title: GT on the spot: How do Yangshan Port immigration officers pair AI screening with sniffer dogs to keep the world's busiest gateway moving?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 21:42:00
A section of Shanghai Yangshan Deep Water Port Photo: VCG An overseas cargo vessel slowly approached the port. In the bridge, the captain could not yet make out the coastline with the naked eye, but on a giant screen at the Command Center of the Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station, about 35 nautical miles away, the ship's bright signal had already been firmly detected. The vessel berthed. The gangway was lowered. Crew members disembarked one by one, while their luggage passed through X-ray scanners, their faces were matched, and their travel documents were verified - all in a matter of seconds. At the same time, live footage was fed back to the command center in real time. On both sides of the quay crane, smart sensors automatically captured the body language, clothing and facial features of embarking and disembarking crew, with the data instantly cross-referenced against Border Inspection Clearance Channel and port security gates. This is Shanghai Yangshan Deep Water Port, the world's largest man-made deep-water port built on an island. As a key component of Shanghai Port - which has ranked first in the world in container throughput for 16 consecutive years - Yangshan Deep Water Port handled more than 28 million TEUs (twenty-foot equivalent units) in 2025, accounting for as much as 52 percent of Shanghai Port's total throughput. At this world-class hub that operates around the clock, how can security and efficiency be achieved at the same time? The Global Times reporter recently visited the Phase IV automated terminal of the Yangshan Deep Water Port, and the Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station, to experience firsthand a smart security line woven by "AI algorithms" and the "nose of police dogs." The Command Center of the Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station Photo: Huang Lanlan/GT 'All-seeing eyes' Yangshan Deep Water Port is bigger than many people imagine. More than 20,000 container trucks enter and leave the port area every day, and an average of about 450 authorized boarding personnel conduct work operations daily. Like a set of precision gears spinning at high speed, the terminal has become a vast, tightly coordinated system - one that the local immigration authorities say can no longer be effectively managed by the old-style inspection model that relied on face-to-face, on-site checks. The transformation began with an intelligent sensing system. At the Command Center of the Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station, immigration officer Li Daming demonstrated how the system works. Far out at sea, in the anchorage area, a photoelectric radar covers a radius of 30 nautical miles, bringing every vessel that enters the zone under surveillance. Closer in, detection checkpoints have been set up along the main shipping channel, through which all inbound vessels must pass. "This system has been upgraded over the past few years. It's like installing a pair of 'all-seeing eyes' on the sea," Li told the Global Times. But technology is not always enough. Some deep-sea cargo vessels have complex structures, with tightly packed containers and numerous hidden gaps and interlayers - blind spots that may escape both machines and human eyes. That is why local immigration officers also use another "tool." On an early fall afternoon at local immigration inspection station, the Global Times reporter saw suitcases being lined up on the ground. Hidden inside one of them was a small packet of cannabis. A police dog named "Manman," led by handler Zhang Xiaobin, sniffed its way slowly past the luggage, tail gently swaying. It eventually stopped beside the suitcase concealing the drugs and barked. Four-and-a-half-year-old Manman is a Labrador trained to detect narcotics and has already taken part in multiple real-world operations. In September 2023, the Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station established its police dog unit, which now has seven dogs trained for narcotics detection, explosives detection, patrol and security work, as well as special search-and-rescue tasks. In August 2025, the police dog unit helped uncover contraband during an inspection on a ship's deck. Immigration officers train police dogs to detect narcotics at Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station on August 26, 2026 Photo: Huang Lanlan/GT Better service Yangshan Deep Water Port's bustle is not confined to cargo. In the first half of 2026, more than 4,700 international vessels berthed at the port. Every day, crew members from around the world enter China through this gateway. "The route network here spans more than 200 countries and regions, and the crew come from places such as Russia, the Philippines, India, Ukraine, Sweden and Germany," said immigration officer Wang Jing. To cope with the port's high-density, high-volume operations, Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station has further streamlined clearance procedures to better serve those involved. For those who board ships to visit relatives working as crew members, the process has also become far simpler. "In the past, they had to come to the immigration inspection station in person to apply for a permit. Now, they can do it online," Wang said. Similarly, overseas crew members who need to go ashore only have to obtain a temporary entry permit for seafarers. They can submit their applications online in advance, and on-site immigration officers only need to verify their identity documents against the person present. "As long as it's within the permitted time frame, crew members can easily go shopping or sightseeing in downtown Shanghai," Wang told the Global Times. Data showed that in 2025, Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station processed 10,500 outbound vessel clearances, 259,000 passenger movements and 15,000 crew changeovers. From AI-powered "all-seeing eyes" and drug-sniffing police dogs, to almost contactless clearance, the safety and efficiency of Yangshan Deep Water Port continue to rise. "Every container at this world's largest port is tied to the national port security," Li told the Global Times. "There is no end to port development, and neither will our safeguarding efforts ever stop."

item.title: How China achieved its photovoltaic turnaround
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 21:21:00
Solar rooftop photovoltaic power generation facilities are seen on a building in Qingdao, East China's Shandong Province, on June 23, 2026. Photo: VCG By the end of July, China's installed capacity of solar panels reached 1.286 billion kilowatts in China, surpassing that of coal power for the first time to become the nation's largest power source by installed capacity. In China, photovoltaic (PV) power has shifted from a "satellite-exclusive luxury" to a power source cheaper than coal. This remarkable turnaround offers deep insights into industrial growth and the fundamental laws of energy transition. The essence of this turnaround lies in locking the market and the factories into a single closed-loop system, driving that ecosystem toward systematic synergy and high-efficiency operation. To get this virtuous cycle spinning, the first step was a vigorous push to expand the domestic market. China has been leveraging policy coordination to anchor and open up the domestic market. Measures included shifting subsidies entirely to actual power generation output with 20-year guaranteed terms. This not only plugged loopholes prone to subsidy fraud but also provided stable, long-term revenue streams, turning solar farms into bankable assets that financial institutions were willing to lend to. The foresight of this policy lay not merely in daring to invest when solar costs remained high, but in building a mechanism that forced costs downward rather than simply throwing subsidies at enterprises to keep them afloat. Truly effective industrial policy does not replace the market; rather, it allows market forces to play out fully over long cycles. Once the market opened, cost reduction shifted to continuous technological innovation, driven by compounding, chain-reaction improvements rather than single breakthroughs. Innovations like diamond wire saws slashed silicon wafer costs and established mono-crystalline wafers as the mainstream choice, a trajectory mirrored by PERC solar cell technology. These technologies were not originally invented in China, but why were their industrialization fates ultimately rewritten in Chinese workshops? The reason lies in China's comprehensive, all-inclusive industrial supply chains and intense market competition. The moment a new manufacturing process is successfully verified and run at a single company, domestic equipment suppliers immediately step up with iterative upgrades, and industry peers race to expand production capacity, achieving widespread adoption across the entire sector within a few years. Today, China's PV industry R&D strength has entered the global vanguard. Besides, technology dictates the content of learning, while scale determines its speed. China accounts for over 80 percent of manufacturing output across all segments of the solar supply chain, meaning the vast majority of global PV industrial experience has been accumulated in China. The true weight of China's scaled industrial capacity lies in the fact that its expanding output can, by and large, find genuine, real-world demand to absorb it, be it at home or abroad. When supply can be manufactured and demand can absorb it, costs can slide steadily down the "learning curve." Of course, the industry faces pressing real-world challenges in integration and absorption. On the power grid side, midday surges in solar generation coupled with insufficient support during evening peak hours mean that energy storage deployment and market mechanisms urgently need strengthening. On the industrial side, harmonizing industrial policy with effective measures to curb cutthroat price competition and realigning the supply side with genuine market demand are vital tasks for the period ahead. From a "luxury item on satellites" to a ubiquitous fixture on deserts, rooftops, and fish ponds, solar power has journeyed for over seven decades since the invention of the silicon solar cell. The answer behind China's solar turnaround is hardly a secret: policy guided the market back home, an integrated supply chain system translated innovation into scaled manufacturing capacity, and an ultra-large market and application ecosystem further refined that capacity into seasoned industrial expertise. Chinese enterprises had paid the "tuition fee," and today, the dividends and hard-earned lessons of cost reduction are shared with the world. For the world, the profound significance of China's PV turnaround lies in shattering conventional mindsets: energy security does not have to be entirely tethered to underground reserves and maritime trade routes; at least a portion of it can be forged right inside a workshop.
